groups.source: From zero to just before two seconds, position is two t minus t squared.
groups.caption: From 0 to just before 2 s, position is 2t − t².
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: From two to just before four it stays at zero. From four to just before seven it oscillates as sine of pi t.
groups.caption: From 2 to just before 4 s, it stays at 0. From 4 to just before 7 s, it oscillates as sin(πt).
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: From seven onward it follows seven minus t in the negative direction.
groups.caption: From 7 s onward, it follows 7 − t in the negative direction.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Two t minus t squared becomes two minus two t; constant zero becomes zero.
groups.caption: The derivative of 2t − t² is 2 − 2t. The derivative of the constant 0 is 0.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Sine of pi t becomes pi cosine of pi t by the chain rule.
groups.caption: By the chain rule, the derivative of sin(πt) is π cos(πt).
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Seven minus t becomes minus one.
groups.caption: The derivative of 7 − t is −1.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: At two, four, and seven seconds, the left and right slopes differ, so the ordinary derivative is not defined at those joins.
groups.caption: At 2, 4 and 7 s, the left and right slopes differ. The ordinary derivative is undefined at those joins.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Two minus two t gives minus two, and constant zero gives zero.
groups.caption: Differentiating 2 − 2t gives −2, and differentiating the constant 0 gives 0.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Pi cosine of pi t becomes minus pi squared sine of pi t: the cosine derivative supplies the minus sign and the inner derivative supplies another pi.
groups.caption: Differentiating π cos(πt) gives −π² sin(πt). Cosine supplies the minus sign; the inner derivative supplies the extra π.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.caption: The derivative of the constant −1 is 0.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Dot both sides of displacement equals initial velocity times time plus one half acceleration times time squared with the acceleration vector. The result is scalar.
groups.caption: Displacement is initial velocity times t plus half of acceleration times t². Dot both sides with acceleration to get a scalar equation.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Let A be acceleration length squared, B the dot product of initial velocity with acceleration, and D the dot product of displacement with acceleration. Then one half A t squared plus B t minus D equals zero.
groups.caption: Set A = a·a, B = v₀·a and D = Δr·a, using acceleration, initial velocity and displacement. Then ½At² + Bt − D = 0.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: The quadratic formula gives minus B plus or minus the square root of B squared plus two A D, divided by A.
groups.caption: The quadratic formula gives t = (−B ± √(B² + 2AD)) / A.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: The imaginary unit i satisfies i squared equals minus one.
groups.caption: The imaginary unit i satisfies i² = −1.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Use the exponential with base e, approximately two point seven one eight, and substitute i x into its series: one plus i x plus the square of i x over two factorial, and so on.
groups.caption: Use the natural base e ≈ 2.718. Substituting ix into the exponential series gives 1 + ix + (ix)²/2! + …
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Powers of i cycle through one, i, minus one, and minus i.
groups.caption: The powers starting at i⁰ cycle through 1, i, −1 and −i.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: The real terms form one minus x squared over two factorial plus x to the fourth over four factorial: the cosine series.
groups.caption: The real terms give 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …, the cosine series.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: The coefficients of i form the sine series.
groups.caption: The terms multiplying i give x − x³/3! + …, the sine series.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.

groups.source: Thus e to the i x equals cosine x plus i sine x, Euler’s formula.
groups.caption: So exp(ix) = cos(x) + i sin(x). This is Euler’s formula.
groups.reason: Readable canonical mathematical notation with the same worked example and its conditions.
